strengths: Addresses an important, underexplored practical gap: system-level deployability (latency, memory, bandwidth) of cooperative perception, rather than only accuracy — appropriate as an Applied/Systems contribution.

Comprehensive full-stack solution combining model-side PTQ (with AdaRound-style rounding, block-wise reconstruction) and communication-side codebook quantization, plus a novel alignment module (heterogeneity + spatial losses) that specifically targets multi-agent fusion challenges under quantization.

Real hardware validation: latency, throughput, and power consumption are measured on actual edge platforms (TensorRT/ROS, RTX 3090) rather than purely theoretical FLOP counts, which is rare and valuable for this application domain.

Extensive experiments across three datasets (DAIR-V2X, V2X-Real, OPV2V), six fusion architectures, multiple calibration ablations, and comparisons against strong PTQ baselines (PD-Quant, LiDAR-PTQ) and communication-efficient baselines (Where2Comm, CodeFilling).

The finding that a quantized system can outperform a full-precision system once system-level latency is accounted for (accuracy-latency tradeoff) is a compelling and non-obvious result with practical implications.
Scaling analysis (Fig. 6) convincingly shows quantization enables larger, more accurate backbones to fit within tight in-vehicle GPU memory budgets.
Good transparency in appendix regarding limitations (e.g., V2X-ViT degradation), implementation details, and reproducibility (calibration set size/steps, hardware, LLM-usage disclosure).
weaknesses: Technical novelty is somewhat incremental: most individual components (AdaRound-based PTQ, block-wise reconstruction from BRECQ-like methods, codebook-based messaging from CodeFilling) are adaptations of existing techniques; the main contribution is system-level integration and the alignment module rather than fundamentally new algorithms.

V2X-ViT shows severe accuracy collapse under quantization (e.g., 57.4→29.9 AP30 at INT4/8), indicating the method's generality across architectures is limited; this is acknowledged but not deeply analyzed or mitigated.

System-level latency/communication model relies on specific assumptions (fixed 27 Mbps rate, uniform random asynchronous delay U(0,200)ms) that may not generalize across real V2X network conditions, limiting the strength of the system-level latency claims.

Main system-level experiments (Section 3.2, Table 3) are restricted to PointPillar backbones and INT8/INT8 settings only; the more aggressive INT4 weight results are only validated at the model level, leaving open whether the touted system-level gains hold under more aggressive bit-widths.

The decomposition of the +9.5 mAP30 system-level improvement into contributions from model quantization vs. message/codebook quantization is not clearly isolated, making it harder to attribute gains to specific design choices.

Reproducibility of the real-world testing environment (custom CUDA/TensorRT plugins, ROS pipeline, exact V2X-ReaLO integration) is described only briefly; full release is promised but not verifiable at review time.

strengths: Addresses an important and underexplored problem in V2X cooperative perception: real-world deployability and system-level latency, rather than only accuracy, which is a meaningful shift from the prevailing literature.

Rare and valuable real-hardware system-level evaluation using TensorRT, ROS, and actual edge platforms (vehicle/infrastructure), going beyond the simulated FLOPs/parameter-count proxies common in prior cooperative perception papers.

Comprehensive experimental coverage: three datasets (DAIR-V2X, V2X-Real, OPV2V), six fusion architectures (computation-based, CNN-based, attention-based), and multiple quantization baselines (PD-Quant, LiDAR-PTQ, FP16 low-precision training).

The proposed alignment module (heterogeneity KL loss + spatial L2 loss) is a reasonable, targeted response to a genuine challenge in multi-agent/multi-modal PTQ, and ablations (Table 2) show it meaningfully improves accuracy recovery.
Thorough ablation studies on calibration set size, calibration steps, and codebook configuration (nC, nR), as well as power-consumption measurements, add practical value and reproducibility detail.
The scaling analysis (Fig. 6) illustrating that quantization enables larger backbones to fit within tight GPU memory budgets is a useful and intuitive systems-level argument.
weaknesses: Core technical novelty is modest: the PTQ pipeline largely assembles existing techniques (AdaRound, block-wise reconstruction, max-min calibration), and the codebook-based transmission scheme is adapted directly from CodeFilling (Hu et al., 2024); the main new elements are two relatively simple auxiliary losses (KL divergence and L2) for alignment.

The headline '+9.5 mAP30 improvement over full-precision' claim conflates quantization benefits with system-latency/async-delay effects (Table 3, Section 3.2.2); it is not fully clear how much of this gain is attributable to the quantization method itself versus the benefit of lower bandwidth/latency reducing temporal staleness, making the comparison somewhat apples-to-oranges and potentially overstated as a core contribution of 'quantization'.

No comparison to quantization-aware training (QAT) baselines or more recent/competitive communication-efficient cooperative perception methods beyond Where2Comm and CodeFilling, despite extensive related work discussion of such methods.

Deployment claims are validated on a narrow hardware setup (RTX 3090/specific edge platform); no evaluation on more constrained embedded platforms (e.g., Jetson-class devices) that are more representative of in-vehicle GPUs, which weakens the generalizability of the latency/memory claims central to the paper's motivation.
2-bit quantization, which would stress-test the method's claimed robustness, is explicitly excluded, leaving the practical lower bound of the approach unexplored beyond qualitative justification.

Some architectures (e.g., V2X-ViT) show large degradation even with the alignment module, suggesting the proposed solution does not generalize well to all fusion paradigms, which is acknowledged but not deeply analyzed or mitigated.
Code is not yet released (only promised), limiting immediate reproducibility verification despite claims of being a deployment-ready open system.

strengths: Addresses a genuinely important and underexplored practical problem: most V2X cooperative perception research focuses on FP32 accuracy metrics while ignoring system-level deployability (latency, memory, bandwidth), and this paper is the first to tackle quantization holistically across the full multi-agent pipeline (encoder, fusion, head, and transmitted messages).

Strong empirical evidence at the system level, not just model level: latency is measured on real ROS/TensorRT hardware platforms (vehicle- and infrastructure-side edge devices) rather than purely simulated, and the paper reports a detailed latency breakdown (local/communication/fusion) with a 3.2x total speedup and +9.5 mAP30 gain over full-precision baselines under realistic asynchronous communication modeling.

Good generalizability analysis across six different fusion architectures (computation-based, CNN-based, attention-based), which strengthens the claim that the PTQ pipeline is broadly applicable, while also honestly reporting failure cases (e.g., V2X-ViT).

The proposed alignment module (heterogeneity + spatial alignment losses) is well-motivated by a clear failure mode (BEV feature distribution shift and spatial misalignment under quantization) and is validated with both quantitative ablations (Table 2) and qualitative visualizations (Fig. 3, Fig. 7-8).

Extensive and useful ablations: calibration set size/steps, codebook configurations (nC, nR trade-offs between message size and accuracy), comparisons against strong PTQ baselines (PD-Quant, LiDAR-PTQ) and FP16 low-precision training, plus power/energy consumption measurements, which substantially aid reproducibility and practical understanding.

The scaling experiment (Fig. 6) convincingly demonstrates a practically important benefit: under fixed GPU memory budgets, quantization allows larger/more capable backbones to be deployed than full precision, which is a compelling systems-level argument beyond simple accuracy-vs-compression trade-offs.
Evaluation spans three datasets (DAIR-V2X, V2X-Real, OPV2V) including two real-world benchmarks, improving external validity of the results.
weaknesses: Methodological novelty is somewhat incremental: the core building blocks (PTQ with AdaRound-style learnable rounding, block-wise reconstruction, codebook-based feature quantization following Hu et al. 2024) are adapted from prior work rather than newly invented; the primary contribution is the systems-level integration and the two alignment losses (KL-divergence and L2 on outputs), which are relatively simple additions.

The communication latency model relies on a synthetic uniform delay term U(0,200) ms layered on top of measured transmission time, which is a reasonable approximation but still a simulated component within an otherwise 'real-world' latency claim; this should be flagged more clearly as a modeling assumption rather than a fully measured quantity.

The system still shows substantial degradation for attention-heavy architectures (V2X-ViT drops from 57.4 to 29.9 AP30 at INT4/8), which somewhat undercuts the 'fully quantized, broadly applicable' framing; this is acknowledged as a limitation but is a non-trivial gap for a class of increasingly popular fusion architectures.

No exploration or discussion of quantization-aware training (QAT) as an alternative or complement to PTQ for scenarios where more aggressive compression or better accuracy recovery is needed; the paper positions PTQ as the practical choice but doesn't empirically justify why QAT was not considered given that full training pipelines were already used for the codebook stage.

Extreme low-bit settings (e.g., 2-bit) are dismissed largely via reasoning in the appendix rather than empirical evidence, which is a defensible practical choice but leaves the lower bound of feasible compression somewhat unexplored.

The three-stage pipeline (FP pretraining, codebook learning with two sub-stages, PTQ with calibration) is fairly complex with many hyperparameters (λrec, α, β, T, nC, nR, iteration counts); while ablations are provided for several components, the interacting effects between codebook learning and PTQ calibration are not deeply analyzed, which could affect reproducibility for practitioners without access to the promised code release.

strengths: Addresses a genuinely important and underexplored problem: system-level deployability of cooperative V2X perception, going beyond the accuracy-centric evaluation common in the literature. The framing around local inference, communication, and fusion latency is a valuable contribution to the field.

The proposed system is comprehensive and technically coherent, combining PTQ (with AdaRound, block-wise reconstruction, learnable scale search) with a novel alignment module (heterogeneity + spatial alignment losses) and a learned codebook-based message quantization scheme, unifying model-side and communication-side efficiency in a single pipeline.

Extensive experimentation across multiple datasets (DAIR-V2X, V2X-Real, OPV2V), multiple fusion architectures (computation-, CNN-, and attention-based), and both model-level and system-level (real-world testbed, ROS/TensorRT) evaluations. The ablations on calibration size/steps, codebook hyperparameters (nL, nR), 2-bit quantization, and component-wise contributions (AdaRound vs alignment module) are thorough and support the design choices.

Real-world deployment validation on the V2X-ReaLO platform and power consumption measurements add credibility beyond simulated latency numbers, which is uncommon in this research area and strengthens the practical relevance of the claims.

Clear ablations distinguishing the roles of AdaRound (local weight stability) versus the alignment module (global cross-agent consistency, long-range precision) provide good mechanistic insight rather than just reporting aggregate numbers.

The paper is generally well organized, with a logical progression from motivation to methodology to model-level and system-level experiments, and includes an extensive appendix with additional discussion and qualitative results.
weaknesses: Novelty is somewhat incremental: individual components (PTQ with AdaRound/block reconstruction, codebook-based compression inspired by CodeFilling, KL/L2-based alignment losses) are largely adaptations of existing techniques rather than fundamentally new algorithmic contributions; the primary contribution is systems integration and empirical demonstration rather than a new quantization or compression theory.

The system-level latency model relies on a synthetic communication delay formula (Tcomm = fs/v + U(0,200)) rather than fully real measured end-to-end multi-agent communication under realistic network conditions (packet loss, contention, multi-hop delays), which may limit how representative the reported 3.2x latency and mAP30 gains are of true deployment settings, despite the V2X-ReaLO real-world validation partially mitigating this.

Some accuracy comparisons (e.g., Table 3, System-level Performance) compare QuantV2X against full-precision baselines under different compression assumptions (no compression vs 16x vs codebook), which makes the fairness of certain head-to-head comparisons a bit unclear; a cleaner ablation isolating quantization gains from compression-ratio gains would strengthen the claims.

The paper does not provide code/artifact availability at submission (release is promised but not verifiable), and some implementation details (e.g., exact AdaRound hyperparameters, block reconstruction group sizes, codebook Gumbel-Softmax temperature schedule) are not fully specified, which could hinder exact reproducibility.

Degradation under attention-heavy architectures like V2X-ViT remains substantial even with the proposed alignment module (e.g., AP30 40.0 to 29.9 at INT4/8 in Table 1), indicating the method's generalizability to more complex fusion mechanisms (e.g., LayerNorm-heavy transformers) is limited, though this is acknowledged in the appendix.

The scaling experiment (Fig. 7) and some latency breakdowns lack statistical variance reporting (e.g., confidence intervals across runs), making it harder to assess the robustness of the reported speedup/accuracy figures.

strengths: Addresses an important and underexplored problem for the V2X cooperative perception community: moving beyond accuracy-only evaluation to system-level latency, memory, and bandwidth considerations that matter for real deployment.

Extensive empirical evaluation across multiple datasets (DAIR-V2X, V2X-Real, OPV2V), multiple fusion backbones (Pyramid Fusion, F-Cooper, AttFuse, V2X-ViT, Who2com, Where2comm), and multiple agent modalities, demonstrating that the PTQ pipeline generalizes reasonably well.

Real hardware/testbed validation (TensorRT/ROS deployment, V2X-ReaLO online testbed, power consumption measurements) is a genuine strength rarely seen in cooperative-perception papers and adds practical credibility to the claims.

Thorough ablations in the appendix (calibration set size/steps, codebook nL/nR, AdaRound vs. alignment module decomposition, comparison with PD-Quant/LiDAR-PTQ) that help disentangle the contributions of individual components.

The alignment module (heterogeneity + spatial losses) is a reasonable, well-motivated response to a genuine problem (compounded quantization noise at the multi-agent fusion stage under heterogeneous modalities/backbones and pose noise).
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty: the main components are adaptations/combinations of existing techniques (AdaRound-style rounding, max-min calibration, block-wise reconstruction similar to BRECQ, and a codebook-based message scheme directly built on CodeFilling). The genuinely new piece is largely the alignment module and the systems integration, which is a narrower contribution than the framing ("first fully quantized multi-agent system") suggests.

The headline +9.5 mAP30 and 3.2x latency numbers stem from a simulated system-level latency protocol (Tcomm = fs/v + U(0,200)) rather than fully live concurrent testing; this conflates two distinct effects (model accuracy loss from quantization vs. latency/asynchrony penalty for full-precision baselines) in a way that could be seen as favorable framing rather than a clean comparison of the proposed method's algorithmic contribution.

Table 3 shows QuantV2X (52.6 mAP30) only marginally outperforms CodeFilling (51.4), a prior codebook-only approach that is not quantized at the model level, undermining the claimed necessity/benefit of full end-to-end quantization versus simply adopting an existing communication-efficient codebook scheme.

Several results lack variance/uncertainty reporting (single-run numbers in most tables), and some comparisons (e.g., full-precision baseline with/without compression) are not entirely matched settings, making it harder to assess robustness of the reported gains.

Clarity could be improved: the codebook training/quantization formulation and calibration algorithm are notationally dense, and some claims (e.g., "first fully quantized intermediate fusion system") are stated without sufficiently qualifying prior partial-quantization efforts (e.g., LiDAR-PTQ, CodeFilling) already cited in the related work.

The scaling experiment under GPU memory budgets (Fig. 7) is presented without sufficient methodological detail (e.g., how backbone variants were chosen/trained, whether accuracy-memory tradeoff is fairly matched across both systems), limiting confidence in the generality of the scaling claim.

strengths: Addresses an important, underexplored practical gap: prior V2X cooperative perception work focuses almost exclusively on accuracy, ignoring latency, memory, and bandwidth constraints critical for real deployment. The paper explicitly reframes evaluation around system-level metrics rather than accuracy alone, which is a valuable contribution to the field.

The proposed system is genuinely full-stack: it jointly tackles model-side (PTQ with AdaRound + block-wise reconstruction) and communication-side (codebook-based quantized messaging) efficiency, and shows these two axes have complementary/synergistic effects in the decomposition analysis (Fig. 6).

The alignment module (heterogeneity KL loss + spatial L2 loss) is a sensible, well-motivated technical contribution specific to the multi-agent quantization setting, and ablations (Table 2, Table 10, Table 11) clearly demonstrate its necessity beyond generic PTQ techniques like AdaRound.

Experimental breadth is a major strength: results span three datasets (DAIR-V2X, V2X-Real, OPV2V), six fusion architectures, multiple bit-widths, calibration ablations, comparisons against SOTA PTQ baselines (PD-Quant, LiDAR-PTQ), and codebook hyperparameter sweeps.

Real-world validation is notably strong and rare for this literature: deployment on an actual ROS/TensorRT edge testbed (V2X-ReaLO), reported power consumption measurements, and system-level latency breakdowns measured empirically rather than purely simulated.

The scaling analysis (Section 3.3) showing that quantization allows larger, more capable backbones to fit within fixed GPU memory budgets is a compelling and practically relevant argument for the approach beyond simple compression.
weaknesses: Individual technical components (PTQ with AdaRound-style rounding, block reconstruction, codebook/VQ-based feature compression) are largely adapted from existing quantization and VQ literature rather than fundamentally new; the primary novelty lies in system integration and the alignment module rather than a new algorithmic idea, which is fine for an applied/systems contribution but should be framed accordingly.

Generalizability across fusion architectures is uneven: V2X-ViT suffers severe degradation under INT4 (57.4/49.5 -> 29.9/8.8 AP30/50 in Table 1), which is a substantial failure case that somewhat undercuts the claimed broad applicability of the PTQ recipe, and the paper's explanation (attention/LayerNorm sensitivity) is not deeply investigated or mitigated.

The system-level latency evaluation in Table 3/Section 3.2 relies partly on an analytical communication-delay model (with a synthetic uniform random delay term) rather than being fully measured end-to-end in situ for all baselines, which weakens the strength of the headline 3.2x/+9.5 mAP30 claims relative to the real hardware experiments in the appendix.

The codebook communication scheme assumes a shared, jointly-trained dictionary across agents, which raises open questions about scalability to open-set/heterogeneous agents joining dynamically without retraining—an important practical concern for real V2X deployment that is not discussed.

Extreme low-bit settings (2-bit) collapse dramatically (Table 5), indicating the method's benefits are largely confined to 4-8 bit regimes; this is acknowledged but limits the claimed generality of "fully quantized" as a paradigm.

Comparisons are made mostly against single-agent-oriented PTQ baselines (PD-Quant, LiDAR-PTQ) and older communication-efficient methods (Where2Comm, CodeFilling); no comparison against any concurrent multi-agent-aware quantization method is presented, likely because none exist, but this should be stated more explicitly as a limitation of the comparison landscape.
